identity.title: Servo Pan Sweep
identity.tagline: Turn a knob, the servo points exactly there — manual analog control of a physical angle.

goal: Map a potentiometer's rotation directly onto a servo's angle in real time, so turning the knob smoothly pans the servo — a foundational "analog in, motion out" pattern reused throughout the more advanced robot projects (camera mounts, sensor sweeps, remote-control steering).
simpleSummary: Turn a knob to smoothly aim a servo motor to match.
howItWorks: A servo motor is fundamentally different from the DC motors used elsewhere in this encyclopedia: instead of just spinning, it holds a specific angular position (typically 0-180°) and actively resists being pushed away from it. It expects a repeating pulse on its signal wire roughly every 20 milliseconds, where the pulse's exact width (about 1-2 milliseconds) tells it which angle to hold — a wider pulse means a larger angle. Arduino's Servo library hides all of that pulse-timing detail behind one simple call, write(angle), so this project is really just: read the potentiometer's position with analogRead() (0-1023), rescale that range down to the servo's 0-180° range with map(), and pass the result straight to write().
toolsNeeded: Arduino IDE (free, installed on your computer)
USB cable to connect the board to your computer
circuitDiagramCaption: Servo signal on D9; potentiometer wiper on A0.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the servo's signal wire to D9, power (red) to 5V, and ground (brown/black) to GND.
wiringSteps.detail: A single SG90 can usually be powered directly from the Arduino's 5V pin without issue — see the Obstacle-Avoidance Robot project's troubleshooting if you notice resets or jitter.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the potentiometer's two outer terminals to 5V and GND, and its middle terminal (the wiper) to A0.
wiringSteps.detail: This is the exact same voltage-divider idea as the LDR in Light-Activated Night Lamp, except a potentiometer lets you set the divider ratio manually with a knob instead of it changing with light.

code.explanation: map() is doing the entire conceptual translation here: it takes a value known to fall within one range (the potentiometer's 0-1023) and rescales it proportionally into a different range (the servo's 0-180°) — turning the knob a third of the way produces roughly a 60° servo angle, without any manual arithmetic. The small delay isn't for timing the servo's pulse (the library handles that continuously in the background) — it's just pacing how often a new angle is requested, which is plenty responsive for a knob a human is turning by hand.

expectedBehavior: The servo horn tracks the potentiometer's rotation directly and immediately: turning the knob fully one way points the servo to 0°, fully the other way to 180°, with everything in between mapped proportionally.

troubleshooting.fix: Confirm the Servo library's attach() call ran (check the pin number matches your wiring) and that the servo has power — a servo with a disconnected signal wire but connected power will simply sit still rather than error out.

troubleshooting.issue: Servo jitters or twitches slightly even when the pot isn't moving.
troubleshooting.fix: This is usually electrical noise on the potentiometer's wiper reading — add a small (0.1µF) capacitor between the wiper and GND, or simply ignore small angle changes (a few degrees) in code.

troubleshooting.issue: Servo only moves through part of its range.
troubleshooting.fix: Check the potentiometer is wired with both outer legs to 5V/GND (giving a full-range wiper voltage), not just one outer leg and the wiper.

extensions: Add a second potentiometer and servo for independent pan and tilt (see Joystick Pan-Tilt Turret for the joystick-driven version of this exact idea).
Replace manual potentiometer control with an automatic sweep between two angles.
Mount an ultrasonic sensor on the servo horn and combine with distance readings — see Obstacle-Avoidance Robot.
Smooth the servo's motion by moving one degree at a time toward the target instead of jumping instantly.
